questions.question: What is the purpose of Cypress fixtures and how do you load fixture data in a component test?
questions.answer: Fixtures provide static test data. Use cy.fixture('data.json').as('testData') to load JSON files for component testing.

    E --> F[Component Test]
    F --> G[Assertions]

questions.question: What is the difference between getByRole() and getByText() selectors in Playwright testing?
questions.answer: getByRole() finds elements by accessibility role/name, while getByText() matches by visible text content.

flowchart TD
    A[Start Test] --> B{Need Element?}
    B -->|User Action| C[Use getByRole]
    B -->|Text Content| D[Use getByText]
    B -->|Form Input| E[Use getByLabel]
    B -->|Last Resort| F[Use getByTestId]
    
    C --> G[Auto-wait & Retry]
    D --> G
    E --> G
    F --> G
    
    G --> H[Perform Action]
    H --> I[Assert Results]

questions.question: What is the difference between Selenium WebDriver and Selenium Grid, and when would you use each in your testing strategy?
questions.answer: WebDriver controls single browsers locally; Grid manages multiple browsers across machines for parallel test execution and cross-browser testing.
questions.diagram:
flowchart TD
  A[Test Strategy] --> B{Single Browser?}
  B -->|Yes| C[WebDriver]
  B -->|No| D[Grid]
  C --> E[Local Testing]
  D --> F[Parallel Testing]
  D --> G[Cross-Browser Testing]

questions.question: How would you design a Selenium Grid architecture to handle 10,000 parallel test sessions while preventing memory leaks and stale session accumulation?
questions.answer: Implement distributed hub-node topology with session pooling, health monitoring, and aggressive cleanup strategies.
questions.explanation:
## Architecture Overview
Designing a production-scale Selenium Grid requires careful consideration of session management, resource allocation, and failure handling.

## Implementation Details

**Hub-Node Topology:**
- Multiple regional hubs for load distribution
- Auto-scaling node groups based on demand
- Session affinity for long-running tests
- Health checks every 30 seconds

**Session Management:**
- Session timeout: 300 seconds idle, 1800 max duration
- Session pool with pre-warmed browser instances
- Cleanup every 60 seconds for stale sessions
- Memory monitoring with automatic node restart

**Memory Optimization:**
- Browser process isolation per session
- RAM limits: 2GB per Chrome instance
- Swap optimization for containerized environments
- Garbage collection tuning for JVM heap

## Code Example
```java
// Session cleanup configuration
GridConfig config = new GridConfig();
config.setSessionTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(300));
config.setCleanupCycle(Duration.ofSeconds(60));
config.setMaxSessionDuration(Duration.ofMinutes(30));
config.setMemoryThreshold(0.8); // 80% memory usage triggers cleanup

// Auto-scaling node configuration
NodeConfig nodeConfig = new NodeConfig();
nodeConfig.setMaxSessions(4);
nodeConfig.setMemoryLimit(2048); // MB per session
nodeConfig.setHealthCheckInterval(Duration.ofSeconds(30));
```

## Common Pitfalls
- Forgetting to call driver.quit() in test teardown
- Not monitoring browser subprocess memory usage
- Ignoring WebSocket connection leaks
- Insufficient health check frequency
- Over-provisioning nodes without resource limits
